chunks: Combined vs separate analog, digital, power grounds. The question: What are the tradeoffs between combining analog, digital, and power grounds vs separating them?
Should analog, digital and power circuits get separate grounds or share one solid ground plane? Splitting keeps noisy return currents out of the quiet analog copper.
But every signal that crosses the split loses its return path right beneath it, which makes a big loop.
The usual default is one solid plane, with the board arranged so noisy and quiet currents stay apart.
Imagine a building with a quiet library wing and a noisy workshop wing. A solid wall stops the noise, but anyone carrying things between wings must detour to the single door.
Or you can leave the building open and put the workshop and library at opposite ends, so people rarely cross. A solid plane with careful placement is the open building.
The analogy is loose: the detour matters because current must always complete a loop.
Left, a signal trace crosses the gap between split planes: the high-frequency return current (red dashed) must travel around to the bridge, enclosing a large loop.
Right, the same signal is routed over the bridge so the return runs right beside it and the loop stays small.
Return current: the current flowing back to its source, right under the signal at high frequency ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Split ground: a plane cut into separate analog and digital areas joined at a narrow bridge. Inductance: resistance to sudden changes in current.
A bigger loop has more, about 1 nanohenries per millimeter of detour.
Partitioning by placement: putting analog, digital and power circuits in separate regions of one plane ("When and why to separate grounds").
AGND and DGND pins: a converter chip's analog and digital ground pins. Normally both go to the same plane.
A 3. 3 volts clock edge draws 8 milliamps in 1 nanoseconds. It crosses a split, and its return current must detour 80 mm to the bridge.
At about 1 nanohenries per millimeter that adds about 80 nanohenries, so the spike is L di over dt equals 80 nanohenries times 8 milliamps over 1 nanoseconds equals 0. 64 volts.
Over an unbroken plane the loop is only a few nH, giving about 16 to 40 millivolts. The split made it 16 to 40 times worse. That is the whole idea.
"Combining grounds gives every signal a short, low-inductance return right beneath it, which is simple and robust, but noisy return currents can pass through quiet areas if placement is sloppy.
Separating them keeps noisy currents out of the analog region, but any signal crossing the split loses its return path, which creates loops, crosstalk and EMI.
My default is one solid plane partitioned by placement, with separate grounds only for isolation, very high currents or precision low-frequency work, joined at one deliberate point."
